Ser, ir, dar, ver e hacer no indefinido: Ser, ir, dar, ver, and hacer in the indefinido
PASSO 1: alguns verbos muito usados não: STEP 1: a few very common verbs don't follow lesson 19's pattern. They have their own forms, and it's worth memorizing them as whole words. STEP 2: «ser» and «ir» share exactly the same form in the indefinido: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. The meaning comes from the rest of the sentence: «Fui a Madrid» (I went to Madrid, verb «ir») and «Fue un día largo» (it was a long day, verb «ser»). STEP 3: with «ir», the place follows «a»: «Fuimos a la playa», «Fui al médico» (a + el = al). Never with «en». STEP 4: «dar» and «ver» use the same -er/-ir endings but carry no written accent, because they're one-syllable words: di, diste, dio, dimos, disteis, dieron; vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron. STEP 5: «hacer» swaps its stem for «hic-»; in the third person singular, the «c» becomes «z» to keep the sound: hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron. STEP 6: none of these forms carries a written accent: «fui», «fue», «di», «vi», «dio», «vio». Writing «fuí» or «vió» is a common mistake. STEP 7: in Latin America, these forms are the same. What changes is frequency: there, «Hoy fui al médico» sounds natural, while Spain tends to prefer «Hoy he ido al médico».
o português também tem formas irregulare: English «went» covers both «ir» and, loosely, a sense of «was» in some idioms, but Spanish folding «ser» and «ir» into the exact same form (fui, fue, fuimos…) has no real English parallel — you have to rely entirely on context to tell them apart, the same way context (not form) tells «I was» from «I went» apart in English, just through different words rather than the same one. The spelling trap here is specific to Spanish: these one-syllable forms (fui, fue, di, vi, dio, vio) never carry a written accent, unlike the two-syllable-or-more regular endings from lesson 19 (hablé, habló) which do.
On Sunday I watched a movie with my cousin.
My mother gave me a gift.

Raízes novas: tener, estar, poder, poner: New stems: tener, estar, poder, poner, saber, querer, venir
PASSO 1: um grupo de verbos muda o radic: STEP 1: a group of verbs changes its entire stem in the indefinido and uses its own set of endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. STEP 2: none of these endings carries a written accent. Compare «hablé / habló» (regular, with an accent) and «tuve / tuvo» (irregular, with no accent). STEP 3: the stems to memorize: tener → tuv-, estar → estuv-, poder → pud-, poner → pus-, saber → sup-, querer → quis-, venir → vin-, hacer → hic- (from the earlier section). STEP 4: a full example: «tener»: tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvisteis, tuvieron. «Venir»: vine, viniste, vino, vinimos, vinisteis, vinieron. STEP 5: «estar» in the indefinido says where you were during a closed period: «Estuve en Lima una semana» (I was in Lima for a week). STEP 6: some of these verbs shift meaning in the indefinido, because the fact is a single point in time rather than an ongoing state. «Supe la noticia» means «I found out the news» (at that moment), not «I knew». «Pude venir» means «I managed to come», and «No pude venir» means «I wasn't able to come». «No quise venir» means «I refused to come», with the sense of actively declining. «Conocí a Ana» means «I met Ana (for the first time)», and «conocer» is actually regular in this tense. STEP 7: «tener que + infinitive» (lesson 13) in the past also uses the indefinido: «Tuve que trabajar el sábado». STEP 8: watch the «v»: «estuve» and «tuve» both have a «v», and so does «vine». «Estube» and «tubo» (which is actually the word for a pipe) are both mistakes.
o português tem a mesma ideia: «tive, es: English has the same kind of irregular stem-swap in its own past tense — «go/went», «see/saw», «have/had» are just as unpredictable — so the habit of memorizing an irregular form as a whole word, rather than deriving it, transfers directly. What doesn't transfer is the meaning shift some of these verbs carry in Spanish: English «I knew» and «I could» describe ongoing states, with no separate form for a single, pinpoint moment the way Spanish «supe» (I found out, right then) and «pude» (I managed to, on that occasion) do. That's a real distinction to learn, not just a vocabulary item.
On Thursday I had a hard exam.
We stayed in Lisbon for a week.

Decir, traer e os verbos como pedir e do: Decir, traer, and verbs like pedir and dormir
PASSO 1: «decir» e «traer» têm um radica: STEP 1: «decir» and «traer» have a stem with «j»: dij- and traj-. The endings are the usual ones, but the «i» drops after the «j»: the third-person plural ends in «-eron», not «-ieron». «Dijeron», «trajeron». STEP 2: decir: dije, dijiste, dijo, dijimos, dijisteis, dijeron. Traer: traje, trajiste, trajo, trajimos, trajisteis, trajeron. STEP 3: -ir verbs that change their stem vowel in the present (pedir → pido, dormir → duermo) also change in the indefinido, but only in the third person, singular and plural: «e» becomes «i» and «o» becomes «u». Pedir: pedí, pediste, pidió, pedimos, pedisteis, pidieron. Dormir: dormí, dormiste, durmió, dormimos, dormisteis, durmieron. STEP 4: the same thing happens with «seguir» (siguió), «servir» (sirvió), «repetir» (repitió), «preferir» (prefirió), «sentir» (sintió), «morir» (murió), and «divertirse» (se divirtió). STEP 5: two meaning traps. «Largo» means «long», not «large» — the word for «large» is «grande», and the word for «wide» is «ancho»: «Una calle ancha» (a wide street), «un viaje largo» (a long trip). And «vaso» means «glass» (the drinking kind), not a flower vase (which is «jarrón» or «maceta»): «Pedí un vaso de agua» (I asked for a glass of water).
em português o radical não muda no preté: English past-tense verbs don't change shape between «he asked» and «they asked» — the whole stem-vowel-flip pattern here (e → i, o → u, only in the third person) is new ground with nothing to transfer from English. The real trap, though, is the false-friend pair «largo»/«large»: they look almost identical, but «largo» means «long» and has nothing to do with size or largeness, which is exactly the word an English speaker would reach for by mistake.

Sofía e Pablo conversam na segunda-feira: Sofía and Pablo talk on Monday about their weekend.
— Oi, Pablo. Como foi seu fim de semana?: — Hi, Pablo. How was your weekend?
— Foi longo, mas ótimo. No sábado fui a: — It was long, but great. On Saturday I went to Toledo with my cousin.
— E o que vocês fizeram lá?: — And what did you two do there?
— Vimos a catedral e comemos em um resta: — We saw the cathedral and ate at a small restaurant. My cousin ordered wine and I ordered a glass of water.
— Que bom. Eu fiquei em casa. Tive que e: — Nice. I stayed home. I had to study and couldn't go out.
— Você estudou o domingo inteiro?: — Did you study the whole of Sunday?
— Não. No domingo veio minha irmã e nos: — No. On Sunday my sister came over and brought us some sweets. Then we watched a movie and I slept ten hours.

— Sim, mas agora tenho uma prova e não p: — Yes, but now I have an exam and I didn't set my alarm.
